sentences.text: A grown-up tends the fire in a ring of stones.
First the flames are pale and tall.
Then they settle into orange curls.
A blue tongue flickers close to the wood.
Sparks climb and vanish like brief stars.
The logs tick as heat finds the sap inside.
Marshmallows turn gold, then brown, at the edge of the heat.
Nobody crowds the ring of stones.
Smoke walks off toward the pine trees.
When the flames shrink, embers keep a red glow.
That low glow is quieter than the beginning,
and it lasts long enough for one more story.

questions.prompt: What is this poem mostly about?

choices.text: A campfire changing color as it settles down
A pine tree that learns to cook
A marshmallow that builds a stone ring
A grown-up who puts the fire out at once

questions.explanation: The poem watches the fire from tall pale flames to orange, sparks, and finally quiet embers. The changing fire is the main idea.

questions.prompt: Embers in this poem are what?

choices.text: The pine trees far from the fire
The hot glow left after the flames shrink
The stones before they are stacked

questions.explanation: The poem says that when the flames shrink, embers keep a red glow. Embers are that hot, quieter stage of the fire.
The first line says a grown-up tends the fire in a ring of stones. Nobody else is given that job.

choices.text: The flames are pale and tall

questions.explanation: Pale flames start the poem. Sparks and marshmallows come in the middle. The red ember glow is near the end, before the last quiet story.
